body: https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11542 is on the agenda, after we've applied plenty of comments from two weeks ago and from the community. The explainer and OP are updated.

Notes from this meeting:

- Cross-over between Markers and CSS Highlighting Jake Archibald introduced the potential for crossover between the proposed marker functionality for templating and the CSS Highlight API. Jake Archibald suggested that markers could serve as a declarative way to define a range, which aligns with how the highlighting system works. Noam Rosenthal agreed that if the goal is to use markers for general range highlighting, there is no reason not to do so.
- Marker Implementation and Atomicity Noam Rosenthal discussed the design principle that markers should be atomic, similar to void elements, and not managed as ranges by the browser, because range management is complex and might be too opinionated for the platform. The decision was made for markers to be atomic nodes with metadata to express range capabilities (start, end, or none) without making them non-atomic. Philip Jägenstedt noted that this approach addresses the difficulty of having to read the whole element to know if a marker is part of a range or a single point if it were not explicit.
- Marker Syntax and Attributes Noam Rosenthal explained the proposed marker syntax, which uses pseudo-attributes for future extensibility and is familiar to developers, rather than creating a new CSS-like syntax. The proposed syntax includes `start`, `end`, or nothing for the type, and a `name` for linking markers. Keith Cirkel asked about edge cases like an end marker existing without a start marker, to which Noam Rosenthal responded that if a start marker is missing, the range goes to the end of the element.
- Markers as Declarative Ranges Jake Archibald suggested calling markers "declarative ranges" to clarify their purpose and allow existing range concepts to answer related questions about their behavior, such as when a start is before an end. Noam Rosenthal was open to using the term "range" instead of "marker". Anne van Kesteren questioned whether markers needed to support attribute values like DOM parts, which Simon Pieters confirmed they currently do not.
- Marker Design Scope and Future Use Cases Keith Cirkel suggested that the design should be forward-thinking to avoid an "explosion of new primitives" and that markers could be an on-ramp for developers to learn about ranges, highlights, and DOM parts. Noam Rosenthal agreed that DOM parts could be built on top of markers, which is why they wanted to keep the syntax open to adding future attributes. Keith Cirkel stressed that it is important to think about an on-ramp to all of the other things.
- Marker Syntax in XML Context Olli Pettay raised concerns about the marker syntax in an XML context. Philip Jägenstedt clarified that the current proposal is not thinking about supporting it in XML, but Simon Pieters suggested it could serialize as a comment.
- Alternative Marker Syntax Keith Cirkel proposed an alternative, more HTML-like syntax using a slash at the end for self-closing markers and bang/slash marker syntax for open and close variants, to avoid the word "start". Philip Jägenstedt expressed strong opinions against this, as slashes at the end of elements are typically ignored in HTML, making the syntax feel too XML-like. Noam Rosenthal's main issue with the slash syntax was that it suggests a closing tag, which may be confusing as end markers are selectable nodes. Simon Pieters suggested the `bang slash` syntax would be understandable to web developers and more of a comment than an element.
- Marker Atomicity Discussion Philip Jägenstedt reiterated the rationale for atomic markers, emphasizing concerns about performance overhead with live range object bookkeeping if markers were managed like ranges by the browser. Anne van Kesteren asked for a definition of "atomic," which Philip Jägenstedt clarified as nodes that appear in the DOM and can be moved around, as opposed to ranges where expressing "nonsense" (like moving an end tag) is impossible.
- Alternative Range Naming Proposal Keith Cirkel questioned the necessity of the "start" and "end" markers, suggesting a single named marker where the range could be computed by appending "dash-start" and "dash-end" to the name. Philip Jägenstedt noted that they previously explored a design without explicit start and end, but it required reading the whole element to determine if it was an insertion point or a replacement range. Simon Pieters raised a concern about arbitrary strings after the bang, as sites use these as actual comments, which could lead to compatibility issues or clashes if they become markers.
- Hyperlink IDL Alignment Across Platforms Luke introduced the topic of aligning the hyperlink IDL definition across HTML, SVG, and MathML, which all use hyperlink elements. The current mixin, `HTMLHyperlinkElementUtils`, is broken because the `href` IDL definition conflicts between HTML and SVG. Luke has submitted a PR that moves most of the mixin to a new one, excluding `href` and two algorithms, allowing SVG and MathML to implement their desired behavior.
- Plan for Hyperlink IDL Mixins Luke proposed that the new mixin be used by SVG and MathML, allowing them to define `href` separately. Anne van Kesteren suggested having two mixins: one for `a` and `area` (which includes stringifier behavior for `href`) and a second one for the rest, used by SVG and MathML, with SVG and MathML defining `href` as a standalone thing. Luke confirmed this as the current plan.
- Selected Content Element Updates Anne van Kesteren discussed the issue of selected content elements, confirming agreement with a proposed solution where all selected content elements inside a `select` are always updated. Anne van Kesteren noted that this approach avoids recursion inside the remove operation and simplifies logic around blur and page hide events. Olli Pettay stressed that care must be taken during the looping and cloning process, as each update can run scripts, potentially triggering events like `pagehide` if an iframe is present. Olli Pettay and Anne van Kesteren concluded that the removal process is the tricky case.
- Inconsistencies in Page Hide Events Olli Pettay initiated a discussion on the differences in handling "page hide" events, noting that WebKit, Gecko, and Chromium all have different implementations, with WebKit having a "mysterious custom element thing" that Olli Pettay has no details on. Anne van Kesteren agreed, pointing out that WebKit has "very special code" for actions like `replace all` that deals with iframes and a seemingly non-standard order of page hide events. Noam Rosenthal added that this area is a "very crashy part of the system".
- Compliance of DOM Standard and Web Content Behavior Anne van Kesteren stated they were "pretty sure" the existing implementations do not align with the DOM standard, which they believe is not defensive against scripts running during that time. Noam Rosenthal and Anne van Kesteren discussed that this issue may be rare in actual web content because interacting with parent elements in `page hide` is considered an anti-pattern. Olli Pettay mentioned that Web Platform Tests (WPTs) may not adequately test these mutation cases.
- Interoperability and Standardization Anne van Kesteren concluded that the web platform tests do not reflect the specification, suggesting that there might not be "interoperable behavior on these things" and they are "Definitely not standardized". The participants agreed that they were running overtime and decided to adjourn the meeting.
